questions.stem: What is the main reason for cleaning a kitchen thoroughly?

To remove dirt and germs so food stays safe

essays.stem: Explain the difference between cleaning, disinfecting, sanitising and sterilising, giving a kitchen example of each.
essays.modelAnswer: Cleaning means removing dirt, grease and food waste, usually with hot water and detergent. It does not kill all germs, but germs cannot be removed well while dirt is there. An example is washing a pot with hot soapy water. Disinfecting means reducing germs to a safe level, using a disinfectant chemical or very hot water, on a surface that is already clean. An example is spraying a disinfectant on a cleaned chopping board and leaving it for the contact time on the label. Sanitising, in most kitchens, means using a sanitiser, which is a detergent and disinfectant in one product, to clean and disinfect in one go on lightly soiled surfaces, such as wiping down a bench between tasks. Sterilising means killing all germs, including spores. It needs very high heat, such as steam under pressure, and is not usually done in a kitchen, but a dishwasher's very hot rinse or boiling water come closest. In every case, I follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules.
markingPoints: Cleaning removes dirt and grease with detergent, with an example
Disinfecting reduces germs to a safe level on a clean surface, with an example and contact time
Sanitiser is detergent and disinfectant in one, with an example
Sterilising kills all germs including spores; rarely done in kitchens
Follows the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules

essays.stem: Describe the six stages of cleaning a food preparation surface or a piece of equipment.
essays.modelAnswer: First, if it is electrical, I switch it off and unplug it, and let anything hot cool down. Stage 1 is the pre-clean: I scrape or wipe off loose food and waste into the bin. Stage 2 is the main clean: I wash the surface with hot water and detergent, made up as the label says, using a clean cloth or brush to remove grease and dirt. Stage 3 is the rinse: I rinse with clean, hot water to take off the detergent and loosened dirt. Stage 4 is disinfection: I apply a disinfectant, made up to the right strength, or very hot water, and leave it for the contact time on the label so it can kill the germs. Stage 5 is the final rinse: I rinse off the disinfectant with clean water if the label says it must be rinsed from food-contact surfaces. Stage 6 is drying: I leave it to air dry, or dry it with disposable paper towels, not a tea towel, so germs are not spread again. Then I sign the cleaning schedule.
markingPoints: Pre-clean: remove loose food and waste (after making equipment safe)
Main clean with hot water and detergent at the right dilution
Rinse off the detergent
Disinfect at the right strength for the contact time
Final rinse if the label says, then air dry or paper towel; sign the schedule

essays.stem: Describe how to use cleaning chemicals safely in a kitchen.
essays.modelAnswer: I only use chemicals I have been trained to use and that the Centre supplies for the job. Before I use one, I read the label and the safety data sheet (SDS), which give the dangers, the PPE to wear, the dilution and the first aid. I wear the PPE they say, such as chemical-resistant gloves, eye protection and an apron. I make sure the area has good air flow, by opening windows or using the extractor. I measure the chemical and dilute it exactly as the label says, adding the chemical to the water, not water to the chemical. I never mix different chemicals, especially bleach with ammonia or acid cleaners, because they can give off poisonous gas. If I put a chemical into a smaller bottle, it must be clean and labelled with the name and dilution, and never a food or drink bottle. I keep food covered or moved away while I clean. After use, I put the chemicals back in their own locked store, away from food. If a chemical touches skin or eyes, I rinse with plenty of clean water, follow the SDS and get first aid.
markingPoints: Read the label and the SDS; use only trained-for, Centre-supplied products
Wear the right PPE and keep the area ventilated
Measure and dilute exactly as the label says
Never mix chemicals (bleach with ammonia or acid); labelled containers, never food or drink bottles
Store away from food; correct first aid for splashes as the SDS says

essays.stem: Describe how to clean a meat slicer or a food mixer safely.
essays.modelAnswer: I follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules, and I only clean a slicer if I have been trained. First, I switch the machine off at the switch and unplug it, so it cannot start. On a slicer, I set the blade gap to zero so the edge is covered. I wear a cut-resistant glove when I work near the blade. I take off the removable parts as the maker shows, such as the food carriage, the blade guard and the tray on a slicer, or the bowl, beater and guard on a mixer. I scrape off loose food. I wash the parts in hot water and detergent, rinse them, disinfect them and leave them to air dry. I clean the body of the machine with a cloth that is damp, not wet, wiping the blade from the centre outwards, away from my hand, and never hose or soak the machine because water and electricity can cause shock. When everything is dry, I put the parts back, making sure every guard is fitted correctly. I check it works safely, report any damage, and sign the cleaning schedule.
markingPoints: Switch off and unplug; slicer blade gap set to zero; trained staff only
Cut-resistant glove near the blade; wipe away from the hand
Remove parts as the maker says; wash, rinse, disinfect and air dry
Body wiped with a damp, not wet, cloth; never hosed or soaked
Refit all guards correctly, check, report damage, sign the schedule

essays.stem: Describe how to wash pots, pans and utensils by hand using a three-sink (three-compartment) method.
essays.modelAnswer: First, I clean and disinfect the sinks and draining boards. I fill the first sink with hot water and detergent, at the strength on the label, the second sink with clean hot water for rinsing, and the third sink with a sanitiser at the right strength, or very hot water, as the Centre's method says. I wear gloves to protect my hands from the heat and chemicals. I scrape all food waste from the pots and utensils into the bin. I soak burnt-on food if needed. I wash each item in the first sink with a brush or scourer suitable for the material, inside and out, including handles. I rinse it in the second sink to remove the detergent. I put it in the third sink for the time the sanitiser label or the Centre's method gives. Then I put it upside down in a rack to air dry, without using tea towels. I change the water whenever it becomes dirty, greasy or cool. Sharp knives are washed one at a time, never left hidden in the water. Clean, dry items are stored covered or upside down, in a clean place.
markingPoints: Set up: wash (hot water and detergent), rinse, sanitise sinks, at the right strengths
Scrape food waste first; soak burnt-on food
Wash, rinse, then sanitise for the right time
Air dry in a rack; no tea towels; change water when dirty or cool
Knives washed one at a time, never left in the water; store clean items properly

essays.stem: Explain how to clean and sanitise a reach-in fridge.
essays.modelAnswer: I plan the job for a quiet time. I move the food into another fridge or a cool box, checking the use-by dates and labels, and I throw away anything out of date, unlabelled or spoiled. If the maker says so, I switch the fridge off at the switch. I take out the shelves, racks and drawers and wash them in hot water and detergent, rinse them, sanitise them and leave them to dry. I clean the inside of the fridge from the top down, with hot water and a food-safe detergent, then rinse it and apply a food-safe sanitiser for its contact time. I pay attention to corners, the drain hole and the door seal, which I check for splits or mould and report if it is damaged. I do not use strong-smelling or harsh chemicals that could taint food. I dry the inside, put the shelves back and switch the fridge on. When it is dry and back to 5 °C or below, I put the food back, raw food at the bottom and ready-to-eat food above, oldest at the front. I write the temperature on the log and sign the cleaning schedule.
markingPoints: Move food to another fridge; check dates and throw away unsafe food
Remove shelves and parts; wash, rinse, sanitise and dry them
Clean the inside top-down with a food-safe detergent, then sanitise; no harsh or tainting chemicals
Clean and check the door seal and drain; report damage
Restock only when dry and at 5 °C or below, in the right order; record the temperature and sign the schedule

essays.stem: Explain what a cleaning schedule is, what it should include, and why it is important.
essays.modelAnswer: A cleaning schedule is a written plan, usually a chart on the kitchen wall, that shows all the cleaning that must be done in the kitchen. For each item or area, such as benches, boards, the stove, fridges, floors, drains, hood filters and bins, it should say what is to be cleaned, how often (after each use, daily, weekly or monthly), how to clean it (the method), which chemical to use and at what dilution, the PPE to wear, and who is responsible. It has a space for the person to sign and date when the job is done, and for the supervisor to check it. A cleaning schedule is important because it makes sure nothing is forgotten, including jobs that are done only now and then, such as cleaning behind equipment. It helps keep food safe and stops pests. It shares the work fairly, so everyone knows their jobs. The signed records also show the public health inspector that the kitchen is cleaned properly, and they help the supervisor to spot jobs that were missed.
markingPoints: Defines a cleaning schedule as a written plan of all cleaning
Includes what, how often, how (method), chemical and dilution, PPE
Includes who is responsible, with a signature and supervisor check
Makes sure nothing is missed; keeps food safe and stops pests
Shares the work and gives records for inspections

essays.stem: Describe the signs of pests in a kitchen, how pests can be kept out, and what you should do if you find signs of them.
essays.modelAnswer: The common pests in a Jamaican kitchen are cockroaches, rats, mice, flies and ants. Signs of rats and mice include droppings, gnawed or chewed packets and boxes, smear marks along walls, nests and holes. Signs of cockroaches include live or dead insects, egg cases and a bad smell, often behind stoves, fridges and in drains. Flies and ants can be seen on food and rubbish. To keep pests out, the kitchen is cleaned well every day so there is no food for them. Food is stored in sealed containers, off the floor, and stock is checked when it comes in. Bins have lids and are emptied and cleaned often. Doors are kept shut, windows have fly screens, and holes and gaps in walls are sealed. If I find any sign of pests, I report it to the supervisor at once. I do not spray chemicals on food areas myself. Any food that pests may have touched is set aside and checked, and is thrown away if it is contaminated. The supervisor calls the pest control company, and the area is cleaned and disinfected after treatment.
markingPoints: Names common pests and correct signs (droppings, gnawing, smears, insects, egg cases)
Keep the kitchen clean and food in sealed containers off the floor
Lidded, emptied bins; closed doors, screens, sealed gaps; check deliveries
Report signs to the supervisor at once; do not use pesticides yourself
Throw away contaminated food; pest control called; area cleaned after

essays.stem: Describe how to clean a kitchen floor safely at the end of service.
essays.modelAnswer: I wait until cooking has finished and the floor is clear of people as much as possible. I put out wet-floor signs at the start. I wear non-slip shoes and gloves. I move bins, mats and small equipment out of the way, and I sweep the floor first to remove loose food and rubbish, including under benches and equipment, and put it in the bin. I fill the bucket with hot water and the floor detergent at the strength on the label, using the mop and bucket kept for the kitchen, not the toilet one. I mop from the far corner back towards the door, so I do not walk on the wet floor, and I give extra attention to greasy areas near the stove and fryer. I clean the drain covers and the drains as the schedule says. I change the water when it gets dirty. If the Centre's method says so, I rinse with clean water and push the water to the drain with a squeegee. I leave the signs out until the floor is dry. I rinse the mop and bucket, leave them to dry, and sign the cleaning schedule.
markingPoints: Wet-floor signs out first; non-slip shoes and gloves
Clear and sweep first, including under equipment
Correct detergent dilution and the kitchen's own colour-coded mop and bucket
Mop from the far side towards the exit; extra care near greasy areas; change dirty water; drains cleaned
Signs left until dry; clean and dry the mop and bucket; sign the schedule

essays.stem: Explain how kitchen waste, used cooking oil and recycling should be handled.
essays.modelAnswer: Kitchen waste attracts pests and can spread germs, so it must be handled carefully. Food waste goes into bins with tight lids, lined with bags, and foot pedals if possible, so hands do not touch the lid. Bins are not overfilled. They are emptied often, at least at the end of each shift, and taken to the outside waste area, which is kept clean, covered and away from the kitchen door. The bins are washed and disinfected as the cleaning schedule says. I wash my hands after handling waste. Used cooking oil is never poured down the sink or drains, because it blocks pipes and the grease trap and pollutes water. I let it cool, then pour it into a sealed, labelled container for collection by an approved collector. Cans, bottles, plastics and cardboard are rinsed and sorted into the recycling bins the Centre uses, and cardboard boxes are flattened and taken out of the kitchen so pests cannot hide in them. Broken glass is wrapped and put in a marked container so no one is cut.
markingPoints: Lidded, lined bins, not overfilled, emptied often to a clean outside area
Bins washed and disinfected; hands washed after handling waste
Used oil cooled and stored in a sealed container for collection, never down the drain (reason)
Recyclables rinsed, sorted and cardboard removed from the kitchen
Broken glass wrapped and put in a marked container

practical1.title: End-of-day close-down clean of a kitchen section, using the cleaning schedule
practical1.brief: As a group, carry out the end-of-day clean of one kitchen section, following the Centre's cleaning schedule. The assessor gives each member one area: the stove top, griddle and hood filters (once cool); a reach-in fridge; the preparation benches, boards and shelves; the sinks and hand-wash basin; or the floor and drains (done last). Before you start, the group reads the labels and safety data sheets for the chemicals you will use, and makes up each solution at the right dilution. Each member cleans their area using the six stages of cleaning, wearing the right PPE, and signs the schedule when the assessor has checked it. The fridge member moves and checks the food first and restocks it in the right order when the fridge is back to temperature. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the section is clean and the schedule is signed.
materials: The Centre's cleaning schedule for the section, and a pen
Detergent, degreaser, food-safe sanitiser, floor cleaner, with labels and safety data sheets
Measuring jugs, labelled spray bottles, buckets
Cloths and scourers suitable for each surface, paper towels
Colour-coded mop, bucket and squeegee for the kitchen, broom and dustpan
PPE: chemical-resistant gloves, eye protection, aprons, non-slip shoes
Fridge thermometer or probe, and the temperature log
photos: The group reading the labels and SDS, and the measured dilutions in labelled bottles
Each member at work in the right PPE
The fridge empty and cleaned, then restocked in the right order
The hood filters soaking in degreaser, and the stove top after cleaning
The floor being mopped with wet-floor signs out
Each area after cleaning, and the signed cleaning schedule
checklist: Read the label and SDS and wore the right PPE for each chemical
Measured and diluted the chemicals correctly, and never mixed products
Made electrical and hot equipment safe (off, unplugged, cool) before cleaning
Followed the six stages: pre-clean, main clean, rinse, disinfect, final rinse, dry
Kept food covered or moved away while cleaning, and restocked the fridge correctly
Used the right colour-coded equipment and put out wet-floor signs
Reported any fault or sign of pests to the assessor
Signed the schedule, and put all chemicals and equipment away clean
safety: Read the label and SDS first; wear gloves and eye protection as they say
Never mix chemicals, especially bleach with ammonia or acid cleaners
Switch off and unplug equipment and let it cool before cleaning
Use wet-floor signs and keep walkways clear of buckets and hoses
Lift buckets and fridge shelves with bent knees, keeping the load close; ask for help with heavy items

practical2.title: Clean small equipment, wash up by the three-sink method, and make a chemical safety chart
practical2.brief: As a group, wash up a load of pots, pans, boards and utensils by hand, clean and reassemble the kitchen's small equipment, and make a chemical safety chart. Two members set up the three sinks (wash, rinse, sanitise) at the right strengths and wash up the load, with the others helping to scrape and rack. Each member also takes apart, cleans, sanitises and reassembles one piece of small equipment, with the assessor watching: for example a food processor, blender, stand mixer, can opener or microwave. A slicer is cleaned only by a member the assessor has trained, with the assessor beside them. Together, make a chart on chart paper for the chemicals in the Centre's kitchen, showing for each one: its name, what it is used for, the dilution, the PPE, where it is stored and the first aid, taken from the label and SDS. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the chart is finished and everything is put away.
materials: A load of dirty pots, pans, chopping boards and utensils from a cooking session
Three-sink unit, detergent, food-safe sanitiser, scrapers, brushes, drying racks
Small equipment: food processor, blender, stand mixer, can opener, microwave (and slicer if trained)
The makers' instruction books for the equipment
Cut-resistant glove, chemical-resistant gloves, eye protection, aprons
Labels and safety data sheets for the Centre's kitchen chemicals
photos: The three sinks set up, with the measured solutions
Items being scraped, washed, rinsed and sanitised
The clean items air drying in racks
Each member's equipment taken apart, then the parts being cleaned
Each piece of equipment reassembled with its guards in place
The signed cleaning schedule and the tidy wash-up area
checklist: Set up the sinks at the right strengths and changed the water when dirty or cool
Scraped, washed, rinsed, sanitised and air dried items in the right order
Washed knives one at a time and never left them hidden in the sink
Switched off and unplugged equipment before taking it apart
Cleaned the parts as the maker's instructions say and refitted every guard correctly
Wore the right PPE, including a cut-resistant glove near blades
Gave correct information for their chemicals on the chart
